cards.title: Mendel Rosenblum and John Ousterhout
cards.prompt: In Sprite LFS, where does the permanent copy of a file's data live, and where does the index that finds it live?
cards.answer: Both are in the log. The log is the only structure on disk; the indexing information sits inside the log, so a file is read back out of the log itself rather than out of a separate random-access structure.
cards.body: Storage for the Sprite network operating system, at Berkeley. Their premise was demographic, not clever: memory was getting cheap, caches were absorbing reads, so disk traffic would become writes — and writes are only slow when they seek. So make every write an append and never seek again.

cards.title: The cleaner eats the win
cards.sub: USENIX Winter 1995 · Harvard and UC Berkeley
cards.prompt: Seltzer's TPC-B sweep: at what disk utilization had LFS's advantage over FFS already vanished, and what did the cleaner cost at that point?
cards.answer: 48% utilization — the advantage was gone that early. The cleaner cost a 34% performance degradation, erasing the roughly 50% advantage LFS held with the cleaner switched off.
cards.body: Margo Seltzer and five co-authors ran 4.4BSD-LFS against the 4.4BSD Fast File System on TPC-B, a check-cashing benchmark, sweeping disk utilization. Cleaner off, LFS won handily. Cleaner on, the line flattened onto FFS. No money was ever priced. And TPC-B was not even the workload LFS was built for: the 1991 paper aimed at small files.

cards.title: The Design and Implementation of a Log-Structured File System
cards.prompt: Which two venues published this paper, and how far apart? (Aggregators often list only one.)
cards.answer: The 13th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles in 1991, and ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 10(1), February 1992, pages 26-52. The camera-ready itself says it will appear in both.
cards.body: Open the PDF. Section 3.3 defines segment cleaning in three steps: read a number of segments into memory, identify the live data, write the live data back to a smaller number of clean segments. Sprite LFS used segments of either 512 kilobytes or one megabyte.

cards.title: LSM trees, and the bill Kafka still pays
cards.sub: O'Neil, Cheng, Gawlick, O'Neil · Acta Informatica, 1996
cards.prompt: What did the LSM-tree authors take from LFS, and which specific LFS cost did they claim their structure avoids?
cards.answer: They took the idea of always writing multi-page blocks to new locations, and the name. They claim LSM blocks are freed whole on the trailing edge of the rolling merge, so reuse costs no extra I/O — where LFS blocks are only partly freed, forcing a read and a write to reclaim.
cards.body: The paper that named a whole storage family after Rosenblum and Ousterhout's. Kafka's segment files plus log compaction are the same bargain wearing a retention policy: appends are free, reclaiming space is not, and you pay in rewritten bytes either way. Read your retention config as a cleaning budget.
